Prior research in this domain has predominantly centered on screening strategies and outcome pre-diction (25, 26). To date, however, no systematic review has specifically examined the methodological and design characteristics of interventional clinical trials for diabetic retinopathy. To our knowledge, the present study therefore constitutes the first com-prehensive assessment of diabetic retinopathy clinical trial features. Clinical research on diabetic retinopathy began to show an upward trend around 2005, coinciding with the emergence of the anti-VEGF therapeutic era. Following FDA approval of bevacizumab for oncological indications in 2004 and ranibizumab for neovascular age-related macular degeneration in 2006, the ophthalmology community rapidly initiated exploratory intravitreal injection studies. This paradigm shift fundamentally transformed DR/DME treatment, where laser photocoagulation had previously been the sole standard of care (27).This therapeutic shift stimulated substan-tial clinical investigations into the efficacy, safety, and dosing regimens of anti-VEGF agents. Concurrently, the progressive adop-tion of optical coherence tomography (OCT) provided a standard-ized tool for objective quantitative assessment of retinal thickness, lowering the imaging threshold for clinical trials and further contributing to research growth (28). chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS soft­ ware (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Within-group comparisons of baseline and 12-month BCVA were performed using paired t-tests. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. The association between injection number and visual acuity change was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Treatment switching Treatment switching from bevacizumab to aflibercept was considered in eyes demonstrating inadequate ana­ tomical or functional response. Inadequate response was defined as persistent retinal fluid, insufficient ana­ tomical improvement on OCT assessment, or lack of satisfactory functional improvement, as judged by the treating physician, despite repeated injections. Because of the retrospective real-world design, no rigid quanti­ tative anatomical or visual acuity thresholds were pre­ defined; treatment switching decisions were based on the treating physician's overall clinical judgment integrat­ ing both anatomical and functional response. For eyes undergoing treatment switching, the timing of switching, BCVA before switching, and BCVA after switching were recorded. Treatment switching was unidirectional from bevacizumab to aflibercept during the 12-month study period; no eyes switched back to bevacizumab or under­ went additional therapeutic modifications. Multivariable linear regression To identify independent predictors of visual outcomes, a multivariable linear regression analysis was per­ formed. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR). Independent variables included baseline BCVA, total number of injections during the first year, and treatment switching status. Variables were selected based on clinical relevance and prior literature. Regres­ sion coefficients (β) and corresponding P values were reported. Generalized estimating equation analysis To account for potential inter-eye correlation arising from inclusion of both eyes from some patients, a gener­ alized estimating equation (GEE) model was performed using an exchangeable working correlation structure with robust standard errors. Patient identifier was specified as the clustering variable. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR), and independent variables included baseline BCVA, number of injections, treat­ ment switching status, age, and sex. Data collection Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. Variables included age, sex, number of outpatient visits, total number of intravitreal injections, baseline and 12-month BCVA, and treatment switching status. BCVA was measured using Snellen charts and converted to logarithm of the minimum angle of reso­ lution (logMAR) units using standardized conversion methods. Visual acuity change (ΔlogMAR) was calcu­ lated as the difference between 12-month and baseline values, with negative values indicating visual improve­ ment. Visual outcomes were additionally categorized as improvement (decrease in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR), sta­ bility (change in BCVA between - 0.1 and + 0.1 logMAR), or deterioration (increase in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR). Sensitivity analysis As a sensitivity analysis, the regression model was repeated after restricting the dataset to one randomly selected eye per patient to assess the robustness of the findings. For subgroup analysis, eyes were stratified according to the median baseline BCVA value (1.0 log­ MAR).

Clinical research on diabetic retinopathy began to show an upward trend around 2005, coinciding with the emergence of the anti-VEGF therapeutic era. chunks.document_content: Real-world injection burden, treatment switching, and visual outcomes in diabetic macular edema: a 563-eye cohort study Statistical analysis Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS soft­ ware (version 25.0; IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± stan­ dard deviation, and categorical variables as frequencies and percentages. Normality of distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Within-group comparisons of baseline and 12-month BCVA were performed using paired t-tests. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test. The association between injection number and visual acuity change was evaluated using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Treatment switching Treatment switching from bevacizumab to aflibercept was considered in eyes demonstrating inadequate ana­ tomical or functional response. Inadequate response was defined as persistent retinal fluid, insufficient ana­ tomical improvement on OCT assessment, or lack of satisfactory functional improvement, as judged by the treating physician, despite repeated injections. Because of the retrospective real-world design, no rigid quanti­ tative anatomical or visual acuity thresholds were pre­ defined; treatment switching decisions were based on the treating physician's overall clinical judgment integrat­ ing both anatomical and functional response. For eyes undergoing treatment switching, the timing of switching, BCVA before switching, and BCVA after switching were recorded. Treatment switching was unidirectional from bevacizumab to aflibercept during the 12-month study period; no eyes switched back to bevacizumab or under­ went additional therapeutic modifications. Multivariable linear regression To identify independent predictors of visual outcomes, a multivariable linear regression analysis was per­ formed. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR). Independent variables included baseline BCVA, total number of injections during the first year, and treatment switching status. Variables were selected based on clinical relevance and prior literature. Regres­ sion coefficients (β) and corresponding P values were reported. Generalized estimating equation analysis To account for potential inter-eye correlation arising from inclusion of both eyes from some patients, a gener­ alized estimating equation (GEE) model was performed using an exchangeable working correlation structure with robust standard errors. Patient identifier was specified as the clustering variable. The dependent variable was change in BCVA (ΔlogMAR), and independent variables included baseline BCVA, number of injections, treat­ ment switching status, age, and sex. Data collection Demographic and clinical data were extracted from medical records. Variables included age, sex, number of outpatient visits, total number of intravitreal injections, baseline and 12-month BCVA, and treatment switching status. BCVA was measured using Snellen charts and converted to logarithm of the minimum angle of reso­ lution (logMAR) units using standardized conversion methods. Visual acuity change (ΔlogMAR) was calcu­ lated as the difference between 12-month and baseline values, with negative values indicating visual improve­ ment. Visual outcomes were additionally categorized as improvement (decrease in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR), sta­ bility (change in BCVA between - 0.1 and + 0.1 logMAR), or deterioration (increase in BCVA of ≥ 0.1 logMAR). Sensitivity analysis As a sensitivity analysis, the regression model was repeated after restricting the dataset to one randomly selected eye per patient to assess the robustness of the findings. For subgroup analysis, eyes were stratified according to the median baseline BCVA value (1.0 log­ MAR).
